Do you want to learn how create blazing fast programs, be organized about developing a software project, write C/C++ code that will keep the people who maintain it very happy, learn how to ace an interview in either of these languages since you’ll know them so well, and understand how to properly debug your code when you inevitably run into problems? Students will come away with an understanding of when and why you might want to use C/C++ over another language, how both “low-level” and more abstracted programming can help you, and how to best develop your own software projects in these languages. This course assumes no C/C++ knowledge, but is intended for programmers with some background and experience in other languages.

The standard pattern for `std::condition_variable::wait()` requires that the consumer already holds the lock **before** calling `wait()`. If the unlock and the sleep were two separate steps, the producer could sneak in and call `notify_one()` in between — and the consumer would sleep forever, missing the notification entirely. The idiomatic C++ solution is `std::unique_lock` (not `std::lock_guard`), because `wait()` requires a lock it can release and re-acquire internally.

Content: [P: Philosophy] Rule P.5: P.5: Prefer compile-time checking to run-time checking
Example: // Int is an alias used for integers
int bits = 0; // don't: avoidable code
for (Int i = 1; i; i <<= 1)
 ++bits;
if (bits < 32)
 cerr << "Int too small\n";
This example fails to achieve what it is trying to achieve (because overflow is undefined) and should be replaced with a simple 
static_assert
:
// Int is an alias used for integers
static_assert(sizeof(Int) >= 4); // do: compile-time check
Or better still just use the type system and replace 
Int
 with 
int32_t
.
```cpp
// Int is an alias used for integers
int bits = 0;         // don't: avoidable code
for (Int i = 1; i; i <<= 1)
    ++bits;
if (bits < 32)
    cerr << "Int too small\n";

// Int is an alias used for integers
static_assert(sizeof(Int) >= 4);    // do: compile-time check
```

 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (unsigned i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // risk wraparound
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (auto i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // might not be big enough
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (vector<int>::size_type i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // verbose
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (auto i = vec.size()-1; i >= 0; i -= 2) // bug
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (int i = vec.size()-1; i >= 0; i -= 2) // might not be big enough
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
